title: Open-Source FPGA The "startup idea" to "go big fast"
author: daly

raw.text:
FPGAs are general purpose and can be made to do anything. They are basically a function of the number of repeated elements. They are "commodity items" except for one fact.

The current FPGA manufacturers won't disclose the details of the design internals to "protect their intellectual property".

Only small FPGAs have been reverse engineered and there are some high-quality tools that have been developed. Their limitation is information.

Because of high costs set by the big players the ability to build truly complex FPGA designs (e.g. an NVIDIA competitor or an ARM competitor or a high-function inference chip) is "closed source information" limited.

But by design FPGAs are basicaly simple repeated elements that can be scaled to any size. That means that a new open sourced chip could be a range from really tiny to enormous with cost purely a function of chip die area. This makes it a pure commodity play.

Some "bright spot" student wanting to start a company could get funded to create a new FPGA design (e.g. since wires take up most of the area figure out how to put the wires "under the logic" in a multi-layer design). Extend existing open-source software tools chains for the new chip design. Open-source the design and license it which is what made ARM so big.

Within hours I'm certain the FPGA tools would be updated to full support of the new chip, opening the market to real, high powered chips. Or create your own open-source tools. Build the company around selling expertise like consulting on custom board-level designs using the new chips.

Turning highly capable FPGAs into volume chips is a market nobody has addressed. What it needs is someone who wants to be a startup CEO and someone who has capital to create the first design (probably a few million dollars).

Of course if you have access to REAL capital then buy Xilinx or Altera and open source their design and tool chain. The company that doesn't get bought would disappear overnight. (Somebody call Musk with the idea :-) )

If you know someone who wants to "go big fast" either path is a major opportunity.

title: Show HN: It's now easy to install Linux on an Android Phone – Android2linux
author: brazukadev

raw.text:
Hey HN!

One of my biggest dreams (really) was to have a Linux phone. I tried to install on some phones in the past, even the ones that would be marked as compatible and it was always so difficult that I couldn't really do it. Yesterday I decided to try again, this time using Claude to do most of the work. A couple hours later it runs postmarketOS as my second phone: 4G, SMS, a terminal, SSH.

It took two fixes. U-Boot didn't recognise my phone model, so I patched 14 bytes of its device-tree match strings. Then the modem wasn't working, because the packaged TFTP server that lends the modem a folder mishandled its file-size queries but an upstream build fixed it.

The repo is what came out of it: guides for any phone (but specific just for my xiaomi), an agent skill that follows the same method and safety rules, notes per phone, and web apps reworked for a phone screen (WhatsApp Web for desktop with a one-pane layout).

What doesn't work (in this phone of mine): no charger driver yet (slow charging), no cameras, and no banking apps, so I keep an Android at home for those. Whether this works for you depends on your phone having a port. reports through the issue forms help, especially for phones that don't work yet.

I think that finally succeeding at having a Linux phone is worth creating a post on HN. I was thinking about a Tell HN but decided to convert the knowledge into a repo so more people can share, discuss, add their phones, new apps, etc. Hope it helps!
raw.title: Show HN: It's now easy to install Linux on an Android Phone – Android2linux

title: Ask HN: Are startups today worth it even in a best case scenario?
author: enigmous_hippo

raw.text:
I'm gonna open this with the disclaimer that this is purely a financial and risk comparison post. No one is complaining that we are poorly compensated. It is good to discuss compensation so we can make informed and educated decisions when deciding how to commit the next few years of our lives.

A close friend of mine joined an AI startup (being intentionally vague) around 1.5 years ago and despite the company doing extremely well on valuation, I'm surprised at how he's not really better off than just working at a large tech company.

Concrete numbers for the startup: -200k salary -Equity grant over 4 years is 500k -The company's valuation has since went from single billions to tens of billions, leaving him with a 10x multiplier when looking only at valuation. After you account for dilution, it's closer to 6x. -Liquidity event annually allows you to sell 10% of your vested shares

Big tech at a similar years of experience is around 400-500k total comp, and the RSU component is generally liquid.

For example sake and ease of calculation, if you assume that my friend's entire equity was vested, and he was able to sell 10% of it, it would amount to approximately $300k/liquidity event, which brings him to around 500k a year as well (200k + 300k). In reality, he's really only able to access $300k/4 since that's all he has vested and that brings him closer to $75k for this liquidity event. There are a lot of variables I'm leaving out obviously such as potential future value, IPO, etc., but the thing that is surprising to me overall is that this is a close to best case outcome, yet the employee doesn't really end up any better off than big tech due to lack of liquidity and dilution. I mean I get it, impact, interesting work, etc. -- the qualitative measures -- aren't really accounted for, but I'm not looking to make a wholistic comparison.

This brings me to the question: Is the risk in a startup ever justified for a lower level employee (engineer, Product Manager, Program Manager, etc.)?
raw.title: Ask HN: Are startups today worth it even in a best case scenario?

title: Show HN: Rmux – A lightweight GPU rendered terminal workspace
author: JaTochNietDan

raw.text:
Hey HN,

I've been working on rmux, an open source terminal workspace built in Rust using GPUI and Ghostty's terminal engine.

The main focus has been performance. I wanted something that could handle multiple projects, shells and coding agents without becoming a resource hog or feeling sluggish as more panes are opened, which has been a frustration I've had with some other terminals.

I also have a sweet setup for it to be my standard external terminal for VS Code where I can switch back and forth between the same workspace in VS Code and rmux with a single shortcut. I share the details of how that's done on the VS Code page on the website.

It supports named workspaces, tabs, split panes, keyboard shortcuts and a command palette. Nothing particularly revolutionary in terms of features, but the goal is to make the experience as responsive and lightweight as possible.

Of course the site has a WASM demo - because it's in Rust and that's what the cool people do.

Would be interested to hear what people think, particularly around performance and the overall UX.

Source is on GitHub, linked from the website.
raw.title: Show HN: Rmux – A lightweight GPU rendered terminal workspace
